clue.text: Pitch tents, parking by mid- Kent river

indicators.note: mid- asks for the middle letters of the word that follows it, Kent

parts.note: Kent is an English county in the south-east; only its middle letters are wanted
the Cam is the river that flows through Cambridge
P is the standard abbreviation for parking, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Campers set up their tents beside a river in the middle of the county of Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England; the line-break hyphen in 'mid-' is the setter's middle-letters signal, and 'by' places parking after the river.
explanation.definitionFit: To set up a camp is to pitch tents, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: A conquest, perhaps, and not a soldier to be found?

parts.note: nor means and not
a man is a private soldier, as in officers and men

explanation.surface: Asking whether a victory leaves no soldier anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The Norman Conquest of England in 1066 makes the answer a kind of conquest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norman Conquest of 1066 is the best known example of a conquest qualified by this word.

clue.text: Rival that's not qualified

definitions.meaning: Captain ... is a character in Sheridan's comedy The Rivals, so he is a Rival
unqualified, complete or total, as in total certainty

explanation.surface: A competitor without the required qualifications.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rival' looks like a competitor, but it means a character from Sheridan's play The Rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Absolute appears in The Rivals, and absolute also means unconditional or total.

clue.text: TV quiz team came first in sectional finish

parts.note: a panel is the group of contestants on a TV quiz show
to lead is to come first, so led

explanation.surface: A television quiz team led at the end of one section of the contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sectional finish' sounds like the end of a round, but it is a wall finished in sections.
explanation.definitionFit: Walls finished in panelled wood are covered in separate sections, so the phrase describes this decoration.

clue.text: Hasty hit-and-run

parts.note: a slap is a hit with the open hand
to dash is to run fast

explanation.surface: A careless hit-and-run accident on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'hit-and-run' looks like one crime but splits into two pieces joined by 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done slapdash is careless and rushed, so hasty is a close synonym.

clue.text: Pull out claw

definitions.meaning: to withdraw an entrant from a race or contest
to scrape with claws or nails

explanation.surface: An instruction to pull out a claw.
explanation.definitionFit: To withdraw a horse from a race is to scratch it, and to claw is also to scratch.

clue.text: Keep out of harm's way, in a jam

definitions.meaning: to protect from danger or decay
fruit boiled with sugar, a conserve

explanation.surface: Keeping someone safe while they are in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a jam' looks like an idiom for being in trouble, but 'in a' only links the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep safe is to preserve, and jam is a fruit preserve: verb and noun senses.

clue.text: Roly-poly for each person

definitions.meaning: playfully, round all over, plump in every direction
given to everyone present, as in drinks bought for the whole company

explanation.surface: A pudding served to everyone at table.
explanation.walkthrough: Roly-poly is a British suet pudding as well as a word for plump; here it is the plump sense, read as round all over.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone chubby is round all over, and buying drinks for everyone is buying them for the whole company.

clue.text: Cynical, and not allowing soldiers to take a dip?

definitions.text: not allowing soldiers to take a dip?
definitions.meaning: soldiers are strips of toast dipped in a soft egg, impossible with a firm-cooked one

explanation.surface: A hard-bitten officer who forbids his troops a swim.
explanation.walkthrough: Soldiers are, in Britain, fingers of toast dunked into a soft-boiled egg's yolk.
explanation.definitionFit: A hard-bitten tough person is cynical, and a firm-cooked egg leaves no runny yolk for dipping.

clue.text: One serving in a can?

parts.note: serving looks like dishing out tinned food, but it is serving time, and can is slang for a jail

explanation.surface: Someone dishing food out of a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: An inmate serves a sentence, and can is slang for jail, so this is a playful description of a convict.

clue.text: The fruit of eavesdropping on someone interfering?

indicators.note: eavesdropping means overhearing, so the result is what one hears said

parts.note: a person who interferes in others' affairs is a meddler

explanation.surface: Asking what an interfering busybody gains from listening at doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of eavesdropping' signals a word heard rather than read: MEDDLER said aloud gives the fruit's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The medlar is a small brown fruit, eaten when half rotten, from a tree of the rose family.

clue.text: It'll go off after the designated period

definitions.text: It'll go off after the designated period

parts.words: It'll go off after the designated period
parts.note: go off reads like an alarm clock or food spoiling, but here it means explode after a set delay

explanation.surface: An alarm or a carton of milk that expires on schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: A device with a timer set to explode once a chosen interval has passed.

clue.text: Fashionable sort of house for all to see

parts.note: something in fashion is said to be in
a public house is a pub, so public is a sort of house

explanation.surface: A trendy kind of home on open display.
explanation.walkthrough: A PUBLIC house is the full British name for a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something openly, where everyone can watch, is an idiom for being seen by all.

clue.text: Club takes measure to, get emergency supply

parts.note: an iron is a type of golf club
a ration is a measured allowance

explanation.surface: A golf club takes steps to obtain supplies in a crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' and 'to get' only join the pieces and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An iron ration was the soldier's reserve pack of food kept for emergencies.

clue.text: Slight stutter at first annoys

parts.note: to slight someone is to snub or offend them

indicators.note: at first takes only the opening letter of stutter

explanation.surface: A small speech impediment at the start of a talk irritates listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' looks like an adjective for the stutter but is a verb; 'at first' takes S from stutter.
explanation.definitionFit: To offend people is to upset or irritate them, a verb synonym in the same third-person form.

clue.text: Guitarist's technique caused loss of sleep

definitions.meaning: pressing strings against the frets on a guitar neck
worrying anxiously, what keeps people awake

explanation.surface: Learning the guitar kept someone up at night.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is loose: 'caused loss of sleep' describes the worrying that keeps a person awake.
explanation.definitionFit: Stopping strings on frets is a guitar skill, and anxious worrying is what costs sleep.

clue.text: Sounded doubtful, entering shelter that's most smelly

indicators.note: entering means going into, so the heard word goes inside the shelter

parts.note: a nest is a shelter, as for birds

indicators.note: sounded means said aloud, so the word for doubtful is heard, not spelt

parts.note: iffy is informal for doubtful

explanation.surface: Someone sounding uncertain goes into the smelliest hut.
explanation.walkthrough: Niff is British slang for a bad smell, so niffy means smelly. 'Sounded' signals that the slang word for doubtful is heard, not spelt, and 'entering' puts it in the shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: Niffy is British slang for smelly, so the superlative means smelliest.

clue.text: Old English monster originally recorded in peculiar legend

indicators.note: in places the single letter inside the reshuffled word
peculiar means strange, so the letters of legend are rearranged
originally points to the first letter of the word recorded

explanation.surface: A monster first written down in an odd old tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' gives R, 'peculiar' rearranges LEGEND into GENDEL, and 'in' sets R inside: G-R-ENDEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Grendel is the beast killed by the hero in the Old English epic poem Beowulf.

clue.text: One who attends courses for the handicapped

definitions.text: One who attends courses for the handicapped

parts.words: One who attends courses for the handicapped
parts.note: courses sound like lessons for disabled people, but they are racecourses and the handicap is weight given to horses

explanation.surface: A carer attending classes for disabled people.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who goes to racecourses watches handicaps, races where horses carry weights to level the field.

clue.text: Almost unfeeling, head is a stupid individual

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: numb means without feeling
the skull is the bony head

explanation.surface: A head that is almost numb belongs to a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts the final B from NUMB.
explanation.definitionFit: A numbskull is a dimwit, someone thick-headed.

clue.text: Pete's partner's gone 'off in a huff

parts.note: Peter Cook's comedy partner was Dudley Moore, known as Dud in their Pete and Dud sketches

indicators.note: off means gone bad, so the letters of gone are rearranged

explanation.surface: Pete's partner storms out in a sulk.
explanation.walkthrough: Pete and Dud were the 1960s British comedy double act of Peter Cook and Dudley Moore. 'off' rearranges GONE into GEON.
explanation.definitionFit: Dudgeon is a feeling of offence or resentment, as in high dudgeon, so a huff.

clue.text: Appearing scruffy perhaps, but not subject to search

definitions.meaning: describes hair left untidy and unkempt, never tidied with a brush
to comb an area is to search it thoroughly, so this means not searched

explanation.surface: A messy-looking person who avoids being frisked.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair never tidied looks scruffy, and an area never combed has not been searched: two senses.

clue.text: English deputy takes in new show

indicators.note: takes in means admits or contains, so N goes inside

parts.note: vice is a deputy, as in vice-captain

explanation.surface: An English deputy admits a newcomer to a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes in' puts N inside VICE.
explanation.definitionFit: To evince a feeling is to show or reveal it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Play a part cooking good food, or a total disaster?

annotationWithheld.why: Play a part cooking good food, or a total disaster? (3,2,3): ACT (play a part) + OFGOD needs the anagram of GOOD plus an F, and no clue word properly supplies the F (food has no indicator to take its first letter)
annotationWithheld.clue: Play a part cooking good food, or a total disaster?

clue.text: I am about to stay in the same, place

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the contraction goes round the verb

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm
to bide is to stay or wait

explanation.surface: Someone announcing they are about to remain right where they are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'about to' (going to), but it means around, and 'to' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibidem is the Latin term used in footnotes meaning in the same source, place or work.

clue.text: Persuasive European made advance tackling old question

indicators.note: tackling means taking hold of, so the loan word grips the other pieces

parts.note: to make an advance of money is to lend it, so lent

explanation.surface: A convincing European moves forward to deal with an ancient question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made advance' suggests moving forward, but it is lending money; 'tackling' means gripping, so the loan word holds the old question.
explanation.definitionFit: Eloquent speech is fluent and convincing, hence persuasive.

clue.text: For example, intruding on people in denial

indicators.note: intruding on means pushing into, so the abbreviation goes inside

parts.note: a nation is a people
EG is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: An example of barging in on people who refuse to face facts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For example' looks like an aside introducing the clue, but it supplies its abbreviation, and 'intruding on' puts that inside the people.
explanation.definitionFit: Negation is the act of denying or contradicting, a noun synonym for denial.

clue.text: Kind of skate seen in wave

definitions.meaning: skates on wheels rather than blades are a type named for their ...
a long heavy wave breaking on a beach is a ...

explanation.surface: A fish or a skater spotted riding the surf.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheeled skates take a name from their rollers, and a long swelling sea wave has the same name.
